terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where the demo sends a few events through your emitter.

tasks.title: on, off and emit
tasks.description:
Implement `on`, `off`, `emit` and `listenerCount` on the `Emitter` class in `src/emitter.ts`, and its constructor (it takes an optional `{ onError }`, used in task 3).

- `on(event, listener)` registers a listener and returns a function that removes that registration. Calling the returned function twice is harmless.
- `off(event, listener)` removes the earliest registration of that listener for that event and returns `true`, or returns `false` when there was none.
- `emit(event, ...args)` calls the event's listeners in the order they were added, with the same arguments, and returns `true`. With no listeners it returns `false`.
- `listenerCount(event)` is the number of registrations. Adding the same function twice counts twice and runs twice.

The check calls these in hidden scenarios and compares what ran, in what order, and what each method returned.
nextSteps: Pick a structure that maps an event name to its list of listeners.
Add `off` and the remove function that `on` returns.
Make sure a listener added twice is stored twice.
hints: A `Map` from event name to a collection of listeners covers most of this task.
If you wrap each listener in a small object when you register it, two registrations of the same function stay distinct, and the remove function can point at exactly one of them.
`off` should walk the registrations in order and remove the first whose listener is the same function, then stop.

tasks.title: Listeners that run once
tasks.description:
Add `once(event, listener)` to `Emitter`.

- The listener runs on the next `emit` of that event only, then it is removed.
- It keeps its place in the order among other listeners.
- Like `on`, it returns a function that removes it. `off(event, listener)` with the original function also removes it before it runs.
- If the listener itself emits the same event, it must not run a second time.

The check mixes `on` and `once` listeners and looks at what ran on each emit and what `listenerCount` reports afterwards.
nextSteps: Decide how a registration remembers that it is a once listener.
Make `emit` remove a once registration when its turn comes.
Check that `off` and the returned function find it.
Run the demo and read the second line.
hints: Wrapping the listener in another function makes `off` with the original function stop working. A flag on the registration avoids that.
The order of two steps matters: removing the registration and calling the listener.
Remove the once registration before you call the listener. Then a nested emit no longer finds it.

tasks.title: Safe emits
tasks.description:
Make `emit` safe when listeners change things while it runs.

- A listener added during an emit does not run in that emit. It runs from the next one.
- A listener removed during an emit, before its turn, does not run in that emit. A listener that removes itself must not cause the next one to be skipped.
- A throwing listener does not stop the others. With `new Emitter({ onError })`, call `onError(error, event)` for each error and return normally. Without `onError`, throw the first error after every listener has run.
- A once listener that throws is still removed.

The check also registers 30,000 listeners that each remove themselves during one emit, then 30,000 once listeners, and expects both emits to finish in well under 1.5 seconds.
nextSteps: Loop over a copy of the listeners taken when emit starts.
Before calling each one, check it is still registered.
Wrap each call so an error is collected or reported, not thrown straight away.
Make removing one registration cheap, then rerun the check.
hints: Looping over the live array while listeners remove themselves shifts items under your index. A copy fixes added listeners, but not removed ones on its own.
To know whether a registration is still there in constant time, keep registrations in a structure with fast lookup and delete that also remembers insertion order.
A `Set` of registration objects per event does all of it: `[...set]` is the copy, `set.has(r)` is the still-registered check, `set.delete(r)` is O(1).
